title: The Future God Is Making
reading:
17 For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.

18 But be ye glad and rejoice for ever in that which I create: for, behold, I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy.

19 And I will rejoice in Jerusalem, and joy in my people: and the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her, nor the voice of crying.

20 There shall be no more thence an infant of days, nor an old man that hath not filled his days: for the child shall die an hundred years old; but the sinner being an hundred years old shall be accursed.

21 And they shall build houses, and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them.

22 They shall not build, and another inhabit; they shall not plant, and another eat: for as the days of a tree are the days of my people, and mine elect shall long enjoy the work of their hands.

23 They shall not labour in vain, nor bring forth for trouble; for they are the seed of the blessed of the LORD, and their offspring with them.

24 And it shall come to pass, that before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.

25 The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock: and dust shall be the serpent's meat. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, saith the LORD.
verse: And I will rejoice in Jerusalem, and joy in my people: and the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her, nor the voice of crying.
encouragement: Isaiah's final hope rests in the God who intends to renew His people and the world they inhabit.
emphasis: The images answer real losses.
devotional:
What would an ordinary day look like if the wounds of the world no longer directed it? A family could enjoy its home without fear of displacement. Work could bear fruit without someone else taking it away. Children could grow in safety, and grief would no longer interrupt every hope. Isaiah's closing visions give such concrete shape to the renewal God promises His people.

Chapters 60 through 66 move through glory, human unfaithfulness, prayer, judgment, and hope. Within that movement, Isaiah 65 announces new heavens and a new earth and a Jerusalem made for rejoicing. The Lord Himself delights in His people. The promise reaches into the public life of a community, including its homes, labor, children, and relationships within a creation brought under His peaceful rule.

The images answer real losses. Those who build will inhabit; those who plant will enjoy their harvest. Lives will no longer be marked by the premature destruction that war and oppression bring. The wolf and lamb feed together, recalling the peace pictured earlier in Isaiah. The Lord's holy mountain becomes a place where harm does not define life and His attention is present before His people's prayers are finished.

The passage uses the language of renewed earthly life, including extraordinary longevity. Christian interpreters differ about how these details relate to the stages of God's future kingdom. We can acknowledge those questions while receiving the clear center: the Creator will act, His people will rejoice, and the world's painful disorder will yield to His faithful purpose. The hope rests on His promise rather than our ability to settle every detail.

Isaiah's final chapter keeps the call to humble hearing alongside this expansive future. Judgment remains real, and the Lord regards those who tremble at His word. Ending with hope does not undo the book's exposure of sin. It teaches us why repentance and trust matter within a story whose direction is determined by the holy God who refuses to abandon His redemptive purpose for His people and the nations.

Revelation 21:1-5 takes up Isaiah's new-creation language and brings it to its fullest Christian horizon. God dwells with His people, tears are wiped away, and death itself is gone. The differences in detail deserve attention, yet the connection is unmistakable. Through Christ's victory, the future centers on life with God, whose declaration that He makes all things new gives hope its lasting foundation.

As we leave Isaiah, notice what has changed in your view of God's character. His holiness, judgment, tenderness, and saving promises have belonged together throughout the book. You may carry an unanswered question or a longing that now has clearer words. Bring it into prayer. The story we enter next will face Jerusalem's approaching fall, but we carry with us the hope of the God whose purpose reaches beyond the ruins toward renewal.

The promise reaches into the public life of a community, including its homes, labor, children, and relationships within a creation brought under His peaceful rule.

reflection: Which part of God's promised renewal gives words to a longing I have struggled to express in prayer?
prayer: Father, thank You for the future You are bringing through Christ. Help me honor the grief and injustice still present while trusting Your promise of renewal. Teach me to live with hope, welcome Your searching truth, and long for the day Your presence fills the world with peace. Amen.

title: Known Before the First Difficult Word
reading:
4 Then the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

5 Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.

6 Then said I, Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.

7 But the LORD said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak.

8 Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the LORD.

9 Then the LORD put forth his hand, and touched my mouth. And the LORD said unto me, Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth.

10 See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.

11 Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, Jeremiah, what seest thou? And I said, I see a rod of an almond tree.

12 Then said the LORD unto me, Thou hast well seen: for I will hasten my word to perform it.
verse: Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the LORD.
encouragement: God knew Jeremiah's weakness before entrusting him with a difficult word.
emphasis: God's answer to Jeremiah's fear centers on His own presence and authority.
devotional:
Jeremiah's first recorded response to his calling is a protest about his ability to speak. He is young, and the task feels larger than his experience. Many of us know something of that gap between a responsibility and our sense of readiness. His story begins by letting us hear the fear before we watch the costly obedience that follows.

Jeremiah ministers in Judah's final decades before Jerusalem falls to Babylon. The Lord appoints him a prophet to the nations and speaks of knowing him before his birth. This is the account of Jeremiah's particular prophetic commission. His words will announce the uprooting of kingdoms and also the possibility of building and planting, bringing judgment and hope into the same difficult ministry.

God's answer to Jeremiah's fear centers on His own presence and authority. Jeremiah must go where he is sent and speak what he is given. The Lord touches his mouth and places His words there. The prophet's message will not rest on his youth, personality, or rhetorical confidence. Its authority belongs to the God who commissions him and watches over the word He intends to perform.

That dependence will not spare Jeremiah rejection. The book will show him opposed, confined, threatened, and deeply distressed. The Lord's promise to be with him prepares him for faithfulness within those circumstances. Reading the whole story keeps us from equating a divine calling with an easy reception or making the audience's response the final measure of whether truth has been spoken faithfully.

The verbs about uprooting and planting also introduce the book's larger movement. Jeremiah will expose the failure of Judah's covenant life and announce Babylon's coming judgment. Yet beyond the destruction, God will promise return and a new covenant. The young prophet's difficult words belong within a redemptive purpose he cannot see in full at the beginning of his assignment before the Lord.

In 2 Timothy 1:6-12, Paul encourages Timothy to bear witness to Christ with power, love, and a sound mind. The gospel's hope rests in God's grace and the appearing of the Savior who has defeated death. Timothy's work differs from Jeremiah's prophetic office, but both passages locate courage in dependence on God rather than a claim to personal adequacy before difficult hearers.

Our own responsibilities require discernment. A strong feeling does not make our words a prophetic message, and humility includes checking our understanding and receiving counsel. Still, there are ordinary occasions for truthful, loving speech that fear can make difficult. Bring one of those occasions before Christ. Ask for the willingness to listen, the restraint to speak carefully, and the courage to remain faithful without needing to control how another person responds.
context: Jeremiah ministers in Judah's final decades before Jerusalem falls to Babylon. The Lord appoints him a prophet to the nations and speaks of knowing him before his birth. This is the account of Jeremiah's particular prophetic commission. His words will announce the uprooting of kingdoms and also the possibility of building and planting, bringing judgment and hope into the same difficult ministry.

The gospel's hope rests in God's grace and the appearing of the Savior who has defeated death. reflection: What responsibility or conversation might I bring before God with greater honesty about both my fear and my dependence on Him?
prayer: Father, You know my limitations and the responsibilities before me. Help me listen carefully to Scripture and speak with humility, love, and courage. Thank You for the grace given in Christ. Keep me willing to learn and faithful in the work that is actually mine to do. Amen.

title: The Thirst Our Cisterns Cannot Satisfy
reading:
9 Wherefore I will yet plead with you, saith the LORD, and with your children's children will I plead.

10 For pass over the isles of Chittim, and see; and send unto Kedar, and consider diligently, and see if there be such a thing.

11 Hath a nation changed their gods, which are yet no gods? but my people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit.

12 Be astonished, O ye heavens, at this, and be horribly afraid, be ye very desolate, saith the LORD.

13 For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
verse: For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
encouragement: The Lord exposes empty substitutes because He is the living source His people have forsaken.
emphasis: Verse 13 names two evils: forsaking the fountain of living waters and making broken cisterns.
devotional:
Imagine working hard to build a reservoir, only to watch the water disappear through cracks you cannot seal. Each repair requires more effort, yet the thirst remains. Jeremiah uses that picture to explain Judah's spiritual condition. The problem includes both the substitute they have chosen and the living source they have abandoned while trying to secure life another way.

Jeremiah 2 remembers the Lord's relationship with His people and confronts their exchange of His glory for what cannot profit them. Other nations remain loyal to their gods, though those gods are powerless, while Judah turns away from the living God. The heavens are summoned to witness the astonishing betrayal. The accusation is grounded in a history of divine faithfulness that makes this exchange especially grievous.

Verse 13 names two evils: forsaking the fountain of living waters and making broken cisterns. A spring provides water from its own continuing supply; a cistern depends on what is put into it and loses that supply when damaged. Judah has sought security through idols and political loyalties that cannot give the life or protection the people expect. Their own labor deepens dependence on something fundamentally unable to sustain them.

The following chapter continues the Lord's call to return, using the language of covenant unfaithfulness. His concern reaches into the heart of their attachment. Merely adjusting a religious habit will not address the source of their wandering. The people need to recognize whom they have left and receive His invitation to come back. Repentance becomes a relational turning toward the God who has not forgotten them.

We can recognize a similar pattern without making every valued part of life an idol. Work, friendship, rest, and financial planning are good gifts. They become strained when we ask them to give us an identity, security, or satisfaction that only God can finally provide. The question is what we have come to depend on most deeply, especially when we feel afraid, unwanted, or unable to control the future.

John 4:10-14 brings living water into Jesus' conversation with a Samaritan woman. He offers a gift that becomes a spring of water reaching into eternal life. His knowledge of her circumstances makes the invitation personal, and the conversation leads toward worship and His identity as Messiah. The Savior meets genuine thirst with the life He alone can give, opening a relationship beyond the divisions His listeners would ordinarily maintain.

Consider where your energy keeps going without yielding the rest you hoped for. You may need practical changes, but you can also ask what expectation sits beneath the effort. Bring that expectation before Jesus. There is no need to disguise the thirst itself. Jeremiah's image can help us notice the cracks in our substitutes while hearing again the invitation of the living Lord whose presence gives our returning hearts a true source of life.

Other nations remain loyal to their gods, though those gods are powerless, while Judah turns away from the living God. The heavens are summoned to witness the astonishing betrayal. The accusation is grounded in a history of divine faithfulness that makes this exchange especially grievous.

title: When Sacred Places Hide Unchanged Hearts
reading:
1 The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,

2 Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the LORD, all ye of Judah, that enter in at these gates to worship the LORD.

3 Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Amend your ways and your doings, and I will cause you to dwell in this place.

4 Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these.

5 For if ye throughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye throughly execute judgment between a man and his neighbour;

6 If ye oppress not the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, and shed not innocent blood in this place, neither walk after other gods to your hurt:

7 Then will I cause you to dwell in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers, for ever and ever.

8 Behold, ye trust in lying words, that cannot profit.

9 Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery, and swear falsely, and burn incense unto Baal, and walk after other gods whom ye know not;

10 And come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, We are delivered to do all these abominations?

11 Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, even I have seen it, saith the LORD.
verse: For if ye throughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye throughly execute judgment between a man and his neighbour;
encouragement: God's presence calls His people into faithful relationship that reaches beyond the doors of a sacred place.
emphasis: The accusations are specific.
devotional:
The entrance to a familiar place of worship can bring reassurance. We know the building, the people, and the words that will be spoken. Those gifts can support faith, but familiarity can also become a shelter from questions we need to face. Jeremiah stands at the temple gate with a message aimed at that false sense of safety among Judah's worshipers.

The Lord tells him to address people entering to worship. They repeat the phrase about the temple of the Lord as though the building itself guarantees their security. Jeremiah calls them to amend their ways and practice justice. The issue is covenant faithfulness: the God whose name rests on the temple sees the life they lead when they leave its courts and return to their neighbors.

The accusations are specific. They oppress strangers, fatherless children, and widows; shed innocent blood; steal; commit adultery; swear falsely; and follow other gods. Then they stand in the Lord's house as though their presence there excuses what they continue doing. Jeremiah's image of a den of robbers describes a refuge for wrongdoing, where people seek protection without turning from the conduct God has exposed.

The chapter goes on to recall Shiloh, an earlier place associated with God's presence that did not remain protected from judgment. The example warns Jerusalem against treating its privileges as a guarantee that rebellion will have no consequences. God's faithfulness includes the truth of His warnings. His desire for a people who know Him cannot be reduced to the preservation of institutions they assume He must defend.

This word can search us wherever belonging has become a substitute for openness before God. A church history, title, ministry role, or pattern of attendance may have real value and still be used to avoid confession. Grace invites us to bring the whole truth of our lives into the relationship Christ gives. The people harmed by our conduct remain visible to the God we approach in worship.

Mark 11:15-18 deliberately recalls Jeremiah when Jesus confronts the temple's misuse. He combines the call for a house of prayer for all nations with the accusation that it has become a den of thieves. His action stands within the prophetic concern for faithful worship and leads toward escalating opposition. The Lord who searches the temple also gives His life so that sinners can draw near to God through Him.

You may want to consider what gives you confidence when you pray. Is there a practice or role you quietly point to while keeping another matter closed? Bring that possibility to Jesus, whose saving work allows truthful confession. There may be an apology, an act of justice, or a request for help to consider. Let worship become a place where His mercy reaches the life you actually live, including the relationships outside the building's doors.

title: Made to Cling to God
reading:
1 Thus saith the LORD unto me, Go and get thee a linen girdle, and put it upon thy loins, and put it not in water.

2 So I got a girdle according to the word of the LORD, and put it on my loins.

3 And the word of the LORD came unto me the second time, saying,

4 Take the girdle that thou hast got, which is upon thy loins, and arise, go to Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole of the rock.

5 So I went, and hid it by Euphrates, as the LORD commanded me.

6 And it came to pass after many days, that the LORD said unto me, Arise, go to Euphrates, and take the girdle from thence, which I commanded thee to hide there.

7 Then I went to Euphrates, and digged, and took the girdle from the place where I had hid it: and, behold, the girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing.

8 Then the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

9 Thus saith the LORD, After this manner will I mar the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem.

10 This evil people, which refuse to hear my words, which walk in the imagination of their heart, and walk after other gods, to serve them, and to worship them, shall even be as this girdle, which is good for nothing.

11 For as the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, so have I caused to cleave unto me the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, saith the LORD; that they might be unto me for a people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory: but they would not hear.
verse: For as the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, so have I caused to cleave unto me the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, saith the LORD; that they might be unto me for a people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory: but they would not hear.
encouragement: God's strange sign of a ruined garment reveals His desire for a people who remain close to Him.
emphasis: Verse 11 reveals the relationship behind the sign.
devotional:
A treasured object can become a powerful teacher when we see what neglect has done to it. Something once useful lies ruined, and its condition makes the loss difficult to ignore. Jeremiah is given a sign like that. A linen garment worn close to the body becomes the visible picture of a relationship that Judah's pride and refusal to listen have damaged.

The Lord tells Jeremiah to obtain a linen girdle, wear it, hide it, and later retrieve it. When he does, it is spoiled and useless. God explains the action Himself: Judah's great pride will be brought to ruin. The people have refused His words, followed the stubborn purposes of their hearts, and served other gods. The damaged garment gives physical form to the consequence of that unfaithfulness.

Verse 11 reveals the relationship behind the sign. As the garment clings to a person, the Lord intended Israel and Judah to cling to Him. They were to be His people, bringing Him a name, praise, and glory. Their purpose was relational and public: to belong to Him in a way that made His character known. The tragedy is expressed simply in their unwillingness to hear.

The surrounding chapters also let us hear Jeremiah's distress and the opposition his ministry provokes. The sign is delivered within a costly vocation, not a detached lecture about other people's failures. He speaks as someone whose own life is bound to the message. The Lord uses actions and images to confront a people skilled at hearing familiar words without allowing those words to disturb their chosen loyalties.

We can ask what it means to remain close to God without inventing an emotional standard we must maintain every hour. Relationship includes listening, trust, confession, and a response shaped by His truth. Seasons of dryness may still involve genuine faithfulness. The concern in Jeremiah's sign is a willful departure from the Lord, where pride refuses the words through which He calls His people back into shared life with Him.

John 15:1-8 offers a distinct image with a related concern. Jesus describes Himself as the true vine and His disciples as branches who must abide in Him to bear fruit. Their life depends on their connection with Him, and His words are to remain in them. Christ's saving grace gives the relationship its foundation; ongoing dependence makes His life visible through the people who belong to Him.

Consider one habit that helps you attend to Christ and one resistance that makes you close the conversation. Both can become part of prayer. You may need quiet time with a passage, honesty with another believer, or the humility to acknowledge what you have avoided. The ruined garment asks us to take the loss of fellowship seriously while remembering the purpose behind the sign: God desires a people who truly know Him and remain near.

God explains the action Himself: Judah's great pride will be brought to ruin. The people have refused His words, followed the stubborn purposes of their hearts, and served other gods. The damaged garment gives physical form to the consequence of that unfaithfulness.

Their life depends on their connection with Him, and His words are to remain in them. reflection: What does closeness to God mean in the ordinary patterns of my life, and where have I been resisting His words?
prayer: Father, thank You for inviting Your people into a life of belonging to You. Help me see the pride that keeps me distant and receive the words I need to hear. Through Christ, teach me to remain near and let my life reflect the grace You give. Amen.

title: Roots That Reach Beneath the Heat
reading:
5 Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.

6 For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.

7 Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.

8 For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.

9 The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?

10 I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.
verse: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.
encouragement: A life rooted in the Lord can continue receiving His sustaining care when the heat arrives.
emphasis: The tree still encounters heat and drought.
devotional:
Two plants can look similar on a mild day. Their difference becomes clearer when the heat lasts and the rain does not come. What lies beneath the surface begins to matter visibly. Jeremiah uses the contrast between a desert shrub and a tree beside water to describe the deeper loyalties that sustain or diminish a person's life before God.

In Jeremiah 17, the Lord exposes Judah's deeply engraved sin and then contrasts trust in human strength with trust in Him. The person whose heart turns away becomes like a shrub in a parched place. The one whose confidence rests in the Lord is like a tree with roots reaching toward water. Both images address the direction of dependence beneath outward conduct and the life that dependence produces.

The tree still encounters heat and drought. Its blessing is described through the supply reaching its roots and the fruit it continues to bear. This image gives substance to trust without making it a promise of uninterrupted ease. A person's life can be sustained through a difficult season even while circumstances remain painful and the need for practical support, patient endurance, and honest prayer continues to be real.

The next verses bring the heart into view. Human self-understanding is limited because the heart can deceive. The Lord searches what we cannot fully know and responds truthfully to the fruit of our ways. These words invite humility about the explanations we give ourselves. A motive may sound reasonable while being driven by pride, fear, or a desire we have not been willing to bring into the light.

That humility is compatible with thoughtful discernment. We can seek counsel, consider evidence, and pray rather than treating every feeling as suspect or every confident impression as God's direction. Jeremiah draws our attention to the One who knows us completely. His searching knowledge gives us a reason to ask for truth, including truth about a reliance we have mistaken for faithfulness because it has become so familiar.

Luke 6:43-45 uses the image of trees and fruit in Jesus' teaching about the heart. Words and conduct reveal what has been stored within. The connection helps Christian readers move from appearances toward the source of their responses. Through Christ's grace, we can receive forgiveness and ask for a heart increasingly formed by His truth, rather than relying on improved appearances to conceal an unchanged inner life.

Notice a response that has surprised or troubled you recently. It may have revealed exhaustion, a wounded expectation, or a deeper loyalty that needs examination. Bring it before God without rushing to excuse or condemn yourself. Ask what it shows about the roots feeding your life. The Lord who searches the heart also invites trust, giving us a place to seek the sustaining grace we need while the weather around us remains difficult.
context: In Jeremiah 17, the Lord exposes Judah's deeply engraved sin and then contrasts trust in human strength with trust in Him. The person whose heart turns away becomes like a shrub in a parched place. The one whose confidence rests in the Lord is like a tree with roots reaching toward water. Both images address the direction of dependence beneath outward conduct and the life that dependence produces.

title: The Potter's Call to Return
reading:
1 The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,

2 Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words.

3 Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels.

4 And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.

5 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

6 O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.

7 At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it;

8 If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them.

9 And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it;

10 If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them.

11 Now therefore go to, speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I frame evil against you, and devise a device against you: return ye now every one from his evil way, and make your ways and your doings good.

12 And they said, There is no hope: but we will walk after our own devices, and we will every one do the imagination of his evil heart.
verse: O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.
encouragement: The Potter's authority makes Judah's response to His warning a matter of real significance.
emphasis: The command is urgent: each person is to turn from evil and amend their ways.
devotional:
Jeremiah is sent to watch someone work. At the potter's house, a vessel becomes marred in the potter's hands, and he reshapes the clay into another vessel as he considers fitting. The ordinary craft becomes a searching lesson. The Lord explains what the image means for Judah, a people resisting His authority while assuming that their future is already beyond any meaningful response.

God addresses the house of Israel as clay in His hand. He has authority over nations and kingdoms, including the people who bear His name. The verses that follow explain the purpose of the comparison: a threatened nation that turns from evil can receive mercy, while a nation that abandons obedience can face judgment despite a previous announcement of good. Their relationship with Him includes genuine accountability and response.

The command is urgent: each person is to turn from evil and amend their ways. The Potter's sovereignty becomes the ground of a call to repent. Judah's reply is a determination to follow its own plans and stubborn heart. The tragedy is their chosen refusal. They use language of hopelessness while protecting the conduct the Lord is calling them to leave, shutting down the conversation rather than receiving His warning.

This context matters when we use the potter image. It is more searching than a general statement that every painful event is a tool for personal improvement. Jeremiah is addressing national rebellion and the real possibility of mercy in response to repentance. God's authority and human responsibility appear together in the passage. We are meant to hear the Lord's call, not simply admire a picture of being shaped while leaving our response untouched.

The next chapters show opposition hardening around Jeremiah, including public humiliation and his own anguished prayers. The warnings are costly to speak and painful to hear. Yet the invitation to return remains a disclosure of God's concern. He is addressing the people before the judgment arrives, making clear that their choices matter within the relationship they have refused to take seriously before Him.

Romans 9:20-24 also uses potter and clay language, this time within Paul's discussion of God's sovereign mercy and His calling of Jews and Gentiles. Its emphasis differs from Jeremiah's immediate appeal, but both passages humble the assumption that God must answer to our preferred terms. Christians approach this mystery through Christ, receiving mercy as a gift and recognizing the freedom and righteousness of the One who gives it.

There may be a pattern you have described as simply the way you are. Sometimes such language acknowledges a real limitation; sometimes it protects a refusal to change. Bring the distinction before God, with room for wise counsel and patient growth. The Potter's call reaches a people still capable of hearing His warning. Today, the possibility of turning toward Him deserves more attention than the explanation that tells us a response is no longer possible.

The verses that follow explain the purpose of the comparison: a threatened nation that turns from evil can receive mercy, while a nation that abandons obedience can face judgment despite a previous announcement of good. Their relationship with Him includes genuine accountability and response.

prayer: Father, help me receive Your authority with humility and Your invitation with hope. Show me the stubbornness I have called inevitable. Thank You for mercy through Christ. Teach me to turn toward You honestly and to welcome the change Your grace makes possible. Amen.

title: The King Who Will Shepherd Justly
reading:
1 Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! saith the LORD.

2 Therefore thus saith the LORD God of Israel against the pastors that feed my people; Ye have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them: behold, I will visit upon you the evil of your doings, saith the LORD.

3 And I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all countries whither I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they shall be fruitful and increase.

4 And I will set up shepherds over them which shall feed them: and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall they be lacking, saith the LORD.

5 Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.

6 In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely: and this is his name whereby he shall be called, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS.

7 Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that they shall no more say, The LORD liveth, which brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt;

8 But, The LORD liveth, which brought up and which led the seed of the house of Israel out of the north country, and from all countries whither I had driven them; and they shall dwell in their own land.
verse: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.
encouragement: God answers the failure of Israel's shepherds with His promise of a righteous King from David's line.
emphasis: The promise then reaches toward a righteous Branch from David's line.
devotional:
The harm of failed leadership reaches people who may never sit in the room where decisions are made. A neglected responsibility can scatter trust, leave the vulnerable exposed, and make ordinary life feel unsafe. Jeremiah speaks to such failure through the image of shepherds. Those entrusted with the Lord's flock have used their position in ways that destroy the people they were meant to care for.

Jeremiah 21 through 25 confronts Judah's rulers and false prophets as judgment approaches. In chapter 23, the Lord charges the shepherds with scattering His sheep and failing to attend to them. He will hold those leaders accountable and gather His flock from the countries of its dispersion. The people remain His, even when those who claim authority over them have neglected their responsibility before Him.

The promise then reaches toward a righteous Branch from David's line. This King will practice judgment and justice, bringing safety to Judah and Israel. His name points to the Lord as the source of righteousness. The answer to corrupt rule will require more than another confident personality. God's people need a ruler whose character and work truly embody the faithful care their earlier shepherds failed to provide.

The gathering is described as so significant that it will be remembered alongside the exodus. God will bring His people from the north and other places where they have been driven. Jeremiah's message of judgment therefore includes a future shaped by divine faithfulness. The Lord confronts wrongdoing while preserving His purpose for the people and the royal line through which He has promised to bless them.

This passage gives room for both comfort and examination. Someone wounded by negligent leadership can hear that God sees the harm. Someone entrusted with influence can hear that position includes accountability. Most of us occupy both places in different relationships. We receive care and give it, sometimes wisely and sometimes poorly. The promised Shepherd invites us to bring our need for healing and our failures of responsibility into the same truthful prayer.

John 10:11-18 reveals Jesus as the good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. He contrasts His care with the hired worker who abandons them when danger comes. His death and resurrection belong to the work of gathering a flock that knows His voice. Jeremiah's royal hope finds its Christian center in the Savior whose authority is inseparable from His self-giving love and righteous faithfulness.

Consider where trust has been damaged in your experience of leadership. There may be a need for honest conversation, wise boundaries, or help from someone trustworthy. Also consider a person affected by your own decisions. Christ's care allows us to seek restoration without pretending every failure is small. We can receive His mercy and ask that the way we lead, listen, and protect others increasingly reflect the Shepherd to whom every flock ultimately belongs.

He will hold those leaders accountable and gather His flock from the countries of its dispersion. The people remain His, even when those who claim authority over them have neglected their responsibility before Him.

prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for being the Shepherd who gives His life for His sheep. Heal the places where failed care has left fear, and examine the influence I hold. Teach me to receive Your righteousness and serve others with the faithfulness and humility Your grace makes possible. Amen.

title: A Difficult Word in a Hostile Room
reading:
7 So the priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the LORD.

8 Now it came to pass, when Jeremiah had made an end of speaking all that the LORD had commanded him to speak unto all the people, that the priests and the prophets and all the people took him, saying, Thou shalt surely die.

9 Why hast thou prophesied in the name of the LORD, saying, This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolate without an inhabitant? And all the people were gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the LORD.

10 When the princes of Judah heard these things, then they came up from the king's house unto the house of the LORD, and sat down in the entry of the new gate of the LORD's house.

11 Then spake the priests and the prophets unto the princes and to all the people, saying, This man is worthy to die; for he hath prophesied against this city, as ye have heard with your ears.

12 Then spake Jeremiah unto all the princes and to all the people, saying, The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that ye have heard.

13 Therefore now amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the LORD your God; and the LORD will repent him of the evil that he hath pronounced against you.

14 As for me, behold, I am in your hand: do with me as seemeth good and meet unto you.

15 But know ye for certain, that if ye put me to death, ye shall surely bring innocent blood upon yourselves, and upon this city, and upon the inhabitants thereof: for of a truth the LORD hath sent me unto you to speak all these words in your ears.
verse: Therefore now amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the LORD your God; and the LORD will repent him of the evil that he hath pronounced against you.
encouragement: Jeremiah's costly witness keeps open the call to return even in a room determined to reject it.
emphasis: His response keeps the people's opportunity before them.
devotional:
There are rooms in which everyone seems to have agreed what may safely be said. A word that challenges that agreement can change the atmosphere immediately. Jeremiah discovers this after speaking at the temple. The people hear his warning about Jerusalem and respond by threatening his life. The question of whether they will listen becomes a public struggle over the messenger himself.

Jeremiah 26 recounts a temple sermon and its aftermath during Jehoiakim's reign. Priests, prophets, and people accuse Jeremiah of deserving death because he has announced that the temple and city may face devastation like Shiloh. Officials come to hear the case. Jeremiah answers by affirming that the Lord sent him and repeating the appeal at the center of his message: amend your ways and obey God's voice.

His response keeps the people's opportunity before them. Even as he faces danger, he speaks of the mercy they may receive through turning to the Lord. He then acknowledges that his life is in their hands while warning against shedding innocent blood. There is courage here, but also a refusal to let the conflict displace the purpose of the word he has been sent to deliver.

The rest of the chapter recalls earlier prophetic warnings and shows that Jeremiah's preservation involves people who speak and act on his behalf. Another prophet's death is also remembered, preventing us from turning the scene into a simple promise that faithful witnesses always survive. The surrounding chapters continue distinguishing the Lord's word from reassuring messages that people prefer to hear, including promises of a swift end to Babylon's power.

We need that distinction in our own conversations. Opposition by itself does not prove that we are right, and confidence does not establish that our words carry God's authority. Faithfulness includes checking our understanding, receiving correction, and speaking with care. Jeremiah's particular prophetic commission cannot become a shortcut by which we dismiss every challenge to our opinions as resistance to God or proof of our courage.

Acts 4:13-20 shows Peter and John commanded to stop speaking about Jesus. They answer that they must speak of what they have seen and heard. Their witness centers on the risen Christ and a publicly evident healing. The apostles' courage is joined to the truth entrusted to them. Christian readers can learn to value such faithfulness while remembering that the Lord's grace also calls our own manner of speech into account.

Perhaps a necessary conversation is ahead, or one has already left you unsettled. Bring the content and your motives before Christ. Ask what needs to be said, what needs to be heard, and where wise help could clarify the situation. The aim can be a truthful response that serves the relationship and honors God. We can entrust the outcome to Him while resisting the urge to make our own vindication the center of every difficult exchange.

Jeremiah answers by affirming that the Lord sent him and repeating the appeal at the center of his message: amend your ways and obey God's voice.

reflection: When a conversation becomes difficult, what helps me remain both truthful and humble before God rather than defending myself at any cost?
prayer: Father, give me love for truth and humility about my own understanding. Help me speak carefully, hear correction, and remain steady when faithfulness becomes costly. Thank You for the courage and mercy made known in Jesus. Let my words serve others rather than my need to win. Amen.

title: Faithfulness While the Wait Is Long
reading:
4 Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, unto all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon;

5 Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them;

6 Take ye wives, and beget sons and daughters; and take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters; that ye may be increased there, and not diminished.

7 And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.

8 For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Let not your prophets and your diviners, that be in the midst of you, deceive you, neither hearken to your dreams which ye cause to be dreamed.

9 For they prophesy falsely unto you in my name: I have not sent them, saith the LORD.

10 For thus saith the LORD, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.

11 For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.

12 Then shall ye call upon me, and ye shall go and pray unto me, and I will hearken unto you.

13 And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.

14 And I will be found of you, saith the LORD: and I will turn away your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places whither I have driven you, saith the LORD; and I will bring you again into the place whence I caused you to be carried away captive.
verse: And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
encouragement: God's promise of a future gives the exiles a reason to live faithfully within a long and unwanted present.
emphasis: The letter confronts prophets promising something God has not said.
devotional:
Waiting becomes harder when someone keeps promising that it will soon be over. We delay putting down roots, postpone ordinary responsibilities, and measure each day by the escape we expect. Jeremiah sends a letter to people living with that temptation. They are far from home in Babylon, and the word they need will require them to imagine faithfulness during a much longer stay.

Jeremiah 29 addresses Judean exiles who had already been taken from Jerusalem. The Lord tells them to build houses, plant gardens, form families, and seek the peace of the city where they live. They are to pray for Babylon's welfare because their own well-being is bound up with it. This instruction gives substance to daily life in a place they did not choose and cannot yet leave.

The letter confronts prophets promising something God has not said. The exile will last seventy years, and the Lord will then fulfill His good word by bringing His people home. The familiar promise about His thoughts of peace belongs within that long horizon. It assures the community of God's purpose for restoration; it does not give each individual a timetable for immediate success or the removal of every present difficulty.

Prayer remains central during the wait. The people will call upon Him and seek Him with their whole hearts, and He will be found by them. Life in exile can still be life addressed to the Lord. Their distance from Jerusalem does not make faithful work, neighborly concern, or heartfelt prayer meaningless. God's promised future gives those ordinary responses a place within His continuing relationship with His people.

Many circumstances differ from this exile, yet the passage can help us consider how we inhabit an unwanted season. A temporary home, difficult assignment, or extended uncertainty may tempt us to put our whole life on hold. There may be legitimate changes to pursue and still be people to love where we are. Hope can make space for responsible presence while we continue grieving or seeking a different future.

In 1 Peter 2:11-17, believers described as strangers and pilgrims are urged to live honorably among their neighbors. Their identity in Christ shapes practical conduct, regard for others, and reverence for God. The Christian use of exile language develops a related pattern of belonging to the Lord while living responsibly within society. Freedom in Christ becomes a context for faithful service rather than withdrawal from the needs around us.

Consider one ordinary act of care available in your present place. It may be a conversation, responsible work, a prayer for the community, or a relationship worth tending. You can offer it without pretending that every part of the season is good or permanent. The God who addressed the exiles knew both their longing and their location. Bring yours before Him, asking for a hope that remains alive while your actual life continues today.

They are to pray for Babylon's welfare because their own well-being is bound up with it. This instruction gives substance to daily life in a place they did not choose and cannot yet leave.

Their identity in Christ shapes practical conduct, regard for others, and reverence for God. reflection: What would it look like to seek the good of the place where I am while still bringing my longing for a different future before God?
prayer: Father, You know the season I would change if I could. Help me receive today's responsibilities without losing hope. Teach me to care for my neighbors, pray honestly, and trust Your faithfulness through Christ while I wait for a future I cannot arrange on my own. Amen.

title: The Covenant Written on the Heart
reading:
27 Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man, and with the seed of beast.

28 And it shall come to pass, that like as I have watched over them, to pluck up, and to break down, and to throw down, and to destroy, and to afflict; so will I watch over them, to build, and to plant, saith the LORD.

29 In those days they shall say no more, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge.

30 But every one shall die for his own iniquity: every man that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge.

31 Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:

32 Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD:

33 But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.

34 And they shall teach no more every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the LORD: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the LORD: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.
verse: But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
encouragement: God's promise of a new covenant reaches into the heart and rests on His gift of forgiveness.
emphasis: The Lord promises to place His law within His people and write it on their hearts.
devotional:
Knowing an instruction is different from loving what it asks of us. We can understand the rule, repeat it accurately, and still keep our deepest desires moving in another direction. Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant addresses that problem at its root. The hope for God's people reaches beyond their return to a place; it includes a renewed relationship with the Lord who knows their hearts.

Jeremiah 30 and 31 gather promises of restoration amid warnings about judgment. The Lord speaks of building and planting, echoing the terms of Jeremiah's calling. He then announces a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. The earlier covenant, made when He brought their ancestors out of Egypt, had been broken. Their failure is remembered within an announcement of what He Himself will do.

The Lord promises to place His law within His people and write it on their hearts. The familiar covenant relationship remains central: He will be their God, and they will be His people. Knowing Him will extend from the least to the greatest. Forgiveness is essential to that renewed life, with iniquity pardoned and sin no longer remembered against them as the barrier defining their relationship with Him.

This promise does not suggest that God's earlier instruction lacked goodness. It exposes the depth of the human problem and announces a gracious work that addresses it. A ruined city can be rebuilt while the patterns that ruined it remain alive. The Lord promises a restoration that reaches the inner life, where allegiance, desire, and the capacity for a faithful response require His transforming mercy and presence.

The promise first names Israel and Judah, and Christian readers should honor those addressees. The New Testament then explains believers' participation in the new covenant through Christ. We receive that grace through the Messiah who fulfills God's saving purpose, with gratitude rather than any claim to have replaced or exhausted the history of His promises. The story moves forward through His faithfulness and the forgiveness He provides.

Luke 22:14-20 records Jesus at the Passover meal, giving His disciples bread and the cup before His death. He identifies the cup with the new covenant in His blood, shed for them. The relationship Jeremiah promised is brought into focus through His sacrifice. The cross opens forgiveness and belonging that human resolve could never establish, inviting His people into a life sustained by the grace of the crucified and risen Lord.

Perhaps your spiritual effort has become a cycle of determination and discouragement. There may be a specific sin to confess or a desire you need help understanding. Bring those matters before Christ within the promise of forgiveness. Ask for more than an improved appearance: a heart increasingly open to God's truth, a willingness to receive help, and gratitude for the relationship He has made possible through the Son who gave Himself for us.

He then announces a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. The earlier covenant, made when He brought their ancestors out of Egypt, had been broken. Their failure is remembered within an announcement of what He Himself will do.

reflection: Where do I need to receive Christ's forgiveness and ask for a response to God that grows deeper than outward compliance?
prayer: Father, thank You for the new covenant established through Jesus' sacrifice. Help me receive Your forgiveness with gratitude and bring my heart openly before You. Let Your truth shape my desires and relationships as I learn to live as someone who belongs to You. Amen.

title: Buying a Field While the City Falls
reading:
6 And Jeremiah said, The word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

7 Behold, Hanameel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth: for the right of redemption is thine to buy it.

8 So Hanameel mine uncle's son came to me in the court of the prison according to the word of the LORD, and said unto me, Buy my field, I pray thee, that is in Anathoth, which is in the country of Benjamin: for the right of inheritance is thine, and the redemption is thine; buy it for thyself. Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.

9 And I bought the field of Hanameel my uncle's son, that was in Anathoth, and weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver.

10 And I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it, and took witnesses, and weighed him the money in the balances.

11 So I took the evidence of the purchase, both that which was sealed according to the law and custom, and that which was open:

12 And I gave the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Hanameel mine uncle's son, and in the presence of the witnesses that subscribed the book of the purchase, before all the Jews that sat in the court of the prison.

13 And I charged Baruch before them, saying,

14 Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days.

15 For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.
verse: For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.
encouragement: Jeremiah's carefully preserved deed makes God's promised restoration visible while Jerusalem is under siege.
emphasis: Baruch is instructed to preserve the deeds in an earthen vessel so that they will last many days.
devotional:
Some purchases announce confidence in the future. A family plants a tree, someone repairs a long-neglected home, or a community invests in children who will grow beyond the present generation. Jeremiah's purchase is more startling. With Jerusalem under siege and his own freedom restricted, he buys a field in a land about to be lost to the invading army.

Jeremiah 32 describes the Lord preparing him for a visit from his cousin Hanameel. The relative asks Jeremiah to exercise his right to buy family land in Anathoth. Jeremiah recognizes the confirmation of God's word and completes the purchase. Money is weighed, documents are signed and sealed, and witnesses observe the transaction. The details make this a real act within the legal and economic life of Judah.

Baruch is instructed to preserve the deeds in an earthen vessel so that they will last many days. The explanation is a promise: houses, fields, and vineyards will again be possessed in the land. Jeremiah's purchase becomes a public sign of that future. The siege is real, and the coming loss is real, but neither will erase the restoration the Lord has announced for His people beyond exile.

Jeremiah still prays with questions later in the chapter. He acknowledges God's power, Judah's sin, and the army at the city, then brings the surprising command back before the Lord. His obedience and his need for understanding coexist. The following chapter continues the promises of restoration, showing that hope belongs within God's covenant faithfulness rather than a denial of the disaster the prophet has spent years warning about.

We should resist treating this event as general permission for a risky purchase or proof that financial optimism expresses faith. Jeremiah acts on a particular word within his prophetic commission. What we can receive is the pattern of hope grounded in God's actual promise. Faithfulness may have a practical expression while leaving room for grief, questions, and careful discernment about the responsibilities before us in our own different circumstances.

Romans 8:18-25 gives Christians a future grounded in God's redemption through Christ. Creation groans, believers groan, and the hope of bodily redemption is awaited with patience. The passage holds suffering and promised glory together. Because the future is held by the Lord, present life can include both honest lament and acts of faithful care whose full significance may not be visible until much later in the story.

Consider something worth tending even though you cannot see how the season will turn out. It may be a relationship, a person who needs steady care, or a responsibility that seems small beside the uncertainty. Bring it before God with your questions. You do not need to pretend that every outcome is promised. The resurrection of Jesus gives hope a trustworthy foundation from which to receive today's work and the future still beyond our sight.
context: Jeremiah 32 describes the Lord preparing him for a visit from his cousin Hanameel. The relative asks Jeremiah to exercise his right to buy family land in Anathoth. Jeremiah recognizes the confirmation of God's word and completes the purchase. Money is weighed, documents are signed and sealed, and witnesses observe the transaction. The details make this a real act within the legal and economic life of Judah.

The passage holds suffering and promised glory together. Because the future is held by the Lord, present life can include both honest lament and acts of faithful care whose full significance may not be visible until much later in the story.
reflection: What ordinary act of faithfulness might express hope in God's promised future without pretending that today's loss is unreal?
prayer: Father, help me trust Your faithfulness while facing circumstances honestly. Give me wisdom to distinguish Your promises from my preferred outcomes. Through Christ, keep hope alive in me and show me how to live responsibly, generously, and patiently within the unfinished present. Amen.

title: The King Who Tried to Burn the Word
reading:
20 And they went in to the king into the court, but they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, and told all the words in the ears of the king.

21 So the king sent Jehudi to fetch the roll: and he took it out of Elishama the scribe's chamber. And Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes which stood beside the king.

22 Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month: and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him.

23 And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.

24 Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments, neither the king, nor any of his servants that heard all these words.

25 Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them.

26 But the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the LORD hid them.

27 Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, after that the king had burned the roll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah, saying,

28 Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned.

29 And thou shalt say to Jehoiakim king of Judah, Thus saith the LORD; Thou hast burned this roll, saying, Why hast thou written therein, saying, The king of Babylon shall certainly come and destroy this land, and shall cause to cease from thence man and beast?

30 Therefore thus saith the LORD of Jehoiakim king of Judah; He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David: and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.

31 And I will punish him and his seed and his servants for their iniquity; and I will bring upon them, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and upon the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them; but they hearkened not.

32 Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words.
verse: And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.
encouragement: A king can burn a scroll, but he cannot remove the authority of the God whose word it carries.
emphasis: The king's act exposes the difference between controlling an object and answering the truth it contains.
devotional:
Jehoiakim listens to a scroll being read beside a winter fire. After a few columns, he cuts them off and throws them into the flames. The scene is deliberate and unhurried. A king who cannot make the warning disappear from history tries to make it disappear from the room, treating the written word as something his own authority can finally dispose of.

Jeremiah 36 tells how Baruch writes Jeremiah's messages and reads them publicly. Some officials respond with concern and bring the matter to the king. Others urge Jehoiakim not to burn the scroll, but he refuses to listen. He also orders the prophet and scribe seized. Their preservation is attributed to the Lord, whose message has been rejected by the person most responsible for leading Judah in a faithful response.

The king's act exposes the difference between controlling an object and answering the truth it contains. Burning the scroll cannot prevent Babylon's approach or overturn God's judgment. The Lord tells Jeremiah to have the words written again, with further words added. The message remains because its authority belongs to the God who speaks, not to the material on which it was first recorded or the ruler who despises it.

The surrounding chapters also confront broken promises and selective obedience. Leaders may respond to immediate pressure and then return to their former ways when the danger seems to recede. The scroll scene gathers that resistance into a visible action. Jehoiakim rejects a word that calls his world into question, using his power to preserve the version of reality in which he wishes to remain secure.

Our resistance is usually quieter. We can skim a difficult command, search only for interpretations that leave us comfortable, or become absorbed in someone else's failure while avoiding our own. Questions about meaning are legitimate and often necessary. The passage invites us to distinguish patient inquiry from a refusal to hear anything that might change the allegiance or behavior we already intend to protect.

Second Timothy provides a related charge. In 2 Timothy 4:1-5, Paul urges Timothy to proclaim the word with patience and teaching, even when hearers prefer voices suited to their desires. The instruction is given before God and Christ, the coming Judge. Christian faithfulness includes both receiving truth and communicating it responsibly, grounded in the gospel of the Savior who brings mercy while searching the hearts of those He calls to follow Him.

Notice a passage you tend to move past quickly. You may need historical context, a trusted conversation, or time to read it again with care. Bring that need before God alongside any reluctance you recognize. Christ's grace allows us to face correction without making self-protection our first response. The question is whether we are willing to let His Word remain in the room long enough to tell the truth about us and lead us toward Him.

Others urge Jehoiakim not to burn the scroll, but he refuses to listen. He also orders the prophet and scribe seized. Their preservation is attributed to the Lord, whose message has been rejected by the person most responsible for leading Judah in a faithful response.

The instruction is given before God and Christ, the coming Judge. reflection: What part of Scripture am I tempted to set aside because receiving it would disturb a choice or loyalty I want to protect?
prayer: Lord, give me an open heart before Your Word. Help me recognize the truths I avoid and the explanations I use to dismiss them. Let the grace of Jesus make me willing to receive correction, seek understanding, and respond with humility rather than protecting my preferred story. Amen.

title: The Courage of a Man With Old Rags
reading:
7 Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon; the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin;

8 Ebedmelech went forth out of the king's house, and spake to the king, saying,

9 My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon; and he is like to die for hunger in the place where he is: for there is no more bread in the city.

10 Then the king commanded Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, Take from hence thirty men with thee, and take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he die.

11 So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah.

12 And Ebedmelech the Ethiopian said unto Jeremiah, Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords. And Jeremiah did so.

13 So they drew up Jeremiah with cords, and took him up out of the dungeon: and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.
verse: So they drew up Jeremiah with cords, and took him up out of the dungeon: and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.
encouragement: God records the care of someone who noticed a suffering man and took practical steps to help him.
emphasis: The king authorizes a rescue party, and Ebed-melech gathers what is needed.
devotional:
The rescue includes an unexpected detail: old rags. Jeremiah has been lowered into a muddy cistern and left where he may die. When help finally arrives, someone thinks about the ropes cutting into his body and provides worn cloth to cushion them. Scripture pauses over that small act of tenderness within a scene that required considerable courage before the rescuers ever reached him.

Jeremiah 37 and 38 show the prophet confined during Jerusalem's siege. Officials accuse him of weakening resistance and place him in the cistern. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian serving in the royal household, hears what has happened and approaches King Zedekiah. He names the act as evil and explains that Jeremiah may starve. His intervention challenges people whose position could make speaking against them dangerous within the collapsing city.

The king authorizes a rescue party, and Ebed-melech gathers what is needed. He does more than obtain permission or express sympathy. He goes, arranges the ropes, communicates with Jeremiah, and sees him drawn out. The old cloth shows attention to how help is received. A person already suffering need not be handled roughly simply because the rescuers have achieved the main purpose of bringing him back to safety.

This scene interrupts a wider story of leaders refusing the Lord's word. A man whose nationality places him outside Judah's usual circle of identity acts with a regard for justice that many insiders lack. His response is a quiet challenge to assumptions about who will recognize the right thing to do. The coming chapter will reveal that the Lord sees his trust and addresses him personally amid the city's judgment.

Care often requires both moral clarity and practical thought. We may recognize that someone is being harmed but feel unsure how to help responsibly. Seeking advice, involving appropriate support, and noticing the person's actual needs can all belong to love. Ebed-melech's example invites us to consider the details that preserve dignity alongside the larger action required, rather than assuming good intentions alone are enough to make our help gentle or wise.

Matthew 10:40-42 gives weight to receiving Christ's messengers and offering even a cup of cold water to a disciple. Jesus connects such welcome with regard for Himself and the Father who sent Him. The passage helps Christians value practical care offered in His name. The mercy of the Savior reaches into acts that can look ordinary beside more public forms of ministry, yet remain known and significant before Him.

Consider a person who may need both assistance and dignity protected. You might be able to listen, make a call, share a resource, or ask what kind of help would actually serve them. Bring that possibility into prayer. The old rags remind us that tenderness has details. In a story filled with dramatic warnings and national collapse, God preserves the memory of someone who cared how a wounded man was brought out of the darkness.

His intervention challenges people whose position could make speaking against them dangerous within the collapsing city.

title: Remembered in the City's Collapse
reading:
15 Now the word of the LORD came unto Jeremiah, while he was shut up in the court of the prison, saying,

16 Go and speak to Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring my words upon this city for evil, and not for good; and they shall be accomplished in that day before thee.

17 But I will deliver thee in that day, saith the LORD: and thou shalt not be given into the hand of the men of whom thou art afraid.

18 For I will surely deliver thee, and thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.
verse: For I will surely deliver thee, and thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.
encouragement: The Lord who speaks about a city's fall also knows the fear and trust of one person within it.
emphasis: That combination keeps courage human.
devotional:
Large events can make individual lives seem invisible. Reports count losses and describe political changes, while the people within them carry names, fears, and small acts of courage. Jeremiah 39 tells of Jerusalem's fall, but it also preserves a message for Ebed-melech. The man who helped lift Jeremiah from the cistern is personally addressed by the God whose judgment the city is about to experience.

The word comes while Jeremiah is still confined in the court of the prison. The Lord announces that His warnings against Jerusalem will come to pass before Ebed-melech's eyes. Then He promises to deliver him from the people he fears. His life will be preserved because he has put his trust in the Lord. The man who acted courageously is also a man who needs reassurance about his own danger.

That combination keeps courage human. Ebed-melech's intervention did not mean he felt secure or immune to what others might do. Trust took shape through an action offered within fear. The Lord saw both. His promise is particular to this person in this event, revealing the depth of His knowledge while preserving the wider seriousness of what is happening to the city and its unfaithful leadership.

The following chapters continue through aftermath, instability, and further refusals to hear God's word. Jeremiah remains involved in a people whose troubles do not end with the fall of the walls. Baruch also receives a personal word amid these events. Such details show a book concerned with both the fate of nations and the lives of servants who struggle to remain faithful while history moves through painful turns.

We can receive the Lord's attentive knowledge without treating Ebed-melech's rescue as a universal promise of physical safety. Scripture also records faithful people who suffer and die. The assurance Christian readers can carry is rooted in the God who knows their trust and in the saving relationship Christ gives. Acts of love need no public record to become known to Him, even when their earthly outcome remains costly or unseen.

Hebrews 6:9-12 tells believers that God does not forget the work and love shown in serving His people. The passage encourages diligent hope and patient faith within a larger call to perseverance. Our service does not purchase salvation; it belongs within the life that accompanies God's saving grace. Through Christ, ordinary faithfulness can be received as something the Lord sees while we await the fulfillment of His promises.

Perhaps you have grown tired in care that few people notice. Perhaps you are afraid of what a responsible next step may cost. Bring those realities before God with the openness this scene allows. You do not have to choose between admitting fear and trusting Him. Ebed-melech is remembered as a person who did both, and his story invites us to place our names, our care, and our uncertainty within the attention of the Lord who knows.

Then He promises to deliver him from the people he fears. His life will be preserved because he has put his trust in the Lord. The man who acted courageously is also a man who needs reassurance about his own danger.

prayer: Father, thank You that ordinary lives remain known to You. Help me trust Your care without demanding that every outcome follow my wishes. Strengthen the love You have begun in me through Christ, and receive the fears I carry while I continue serving the people before me. Amen.

title: An Unfinished Hope in a Foreign Land
reading:
27 And the king of Babylon smote them, and put them to death in Riblah in the land of Hamath. Thus Judah was carried away captive out of his own land.

28 This is the people whom Nebuchadrezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year three thousand Jews and three and twenty:

29 In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem eight hundred thirty and two persons:

30 In the three and twentieth year of Nebuchadrezzar Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Jews seven hundred forty and five persons: all the persons were four thousand and six hundred.

31 And it came to pass in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, in the five and twentieth day of the month, that Evilmerodach king of Babylon in the first year of his reign lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and brought him forth out of prison,

32 And spake kindly unto him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon,

33 And changed his prison garments: and he did continually eat bread before him all the days of his life.

34 And for his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
